match_question_text: SI unit of charge is _______.

set.explanation_long: Electric charge is measured in Coulombs (C), defined as the charge transported by a current of one Ampere flowing for one second (1 C = 1 A*s). Ampere is the SI base unit of electric current, not charge -- charge is a derived unit. The printed UHS key marks A (ampere), but the ampere is the unit of current; charge is measured in coulombs, so C is kept.

match_question_text: The electrical analog of mass is electricity is _________.

set.explanation_long: In the standard force-voltage analogy between mechanical oscillators and electrical circuits, mass maps to inductance (both resist a change in the equivalent 'velocity'/current), displacement maps to charge, and spring constant maps to inverse capacitance. The printed UHS key marks C (charge), but inductance plays the role of mass (inertia) in electrical circuits, so B is kept.

match_question_text: Which one of the following relations is correct?
Life time of electron in metastable state is about _________.

set.explanation_short: An electron stays in a metastable state for about 10⁻³ s — roughly 100 000 times longer than the 10⁻⁸ s of an ordinary excited state.
set.explanation_long: An ordinary excited state decays by spontaneous emission in about 10⁻⁸ s. A metastable state is an excited state from which the downward transition is 'forbidden', so electrons linger there for about 10⁻³ s. This long lifetime lets electrons pile up in the metastable level, producing the population inversion that a laser needs. (The printed UHS key marks C, 10⁻⁸ s, but that is the lifetime of an ordinary excited state, not a metastable one.)
set.explanation_trick: Ordinary excited state ≈ 10⁻⁸ s; metastable state ≈ 10⁻³ s — the long life is what makes lasers possible.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 10⁻⁵ s is not the textbook metastable lifetime.
explanation_options.b: Correct — electrons remain in a metastable state for about 10⁻³ s.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 10⁻⁸ s is the lifetime of an ordinary excited state.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 10⁻² s is longer than the textbook value.

On a clear day at noon, the intensity of solar energy reaching the earth’s surface is about

set.explanation_short: At the earth's surface on a clear day at noon, solar intensity is about 1.0 kW m⁻²; the 1.4 kW m⁻² figure is the value above the atmosphere.
set.explanation_long: Just outside the atmosphere, sunlight falling at right angles delivers about 1.4 kW m⁻² (the solar constant). Part of this is absorbed and scattered by the atmosphere, so on a clear day at noon about 1.0 kW m⁻² reaches the surface. That is the figure textbooks quote for solar panels and collectors at ground level.
set.explanation_trick: Top of atmosphere 1.4 kW m⁻²; ground level at noon about 1.0 kW m⁻².

explanation_options.a: Correct — about 1.0 kW m⁻² reaches the surface on a clear day at noon.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 1.4 kW m⁻² is the intensity outside the atmosphere, before absorption and scattering.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 1.0 W m⁻² is a thousand times too small.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 1.4 W m⁻² is a thousand times too small.

match_question_text: The path difference ‘BD’ for destructive interference is

set.explanation_short: Waves cancel (destructive interference) when the path difference is an odd number of half wavelengths: (m + ½)λ.
set.explanation_long: When the path difference BD between two coherent waves is a whole number of wavelengths (mλ), crests meet crests and a bright fringe forms. When it is (m + ½)λ — λ/2, 3λ/2, 5λ/2, … — a crest meets a trough and the waves cancel, giving a dark fringe. In Young's experiment the path difference itself equals d sin θ, which is only the general expression, not the condition for darkness.

explanation_options.a: Correct — destructive interference needs a path difference of (m + ½)λ.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — mλ is the condition for constructive interference.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — d sin θ is the path difference itself, not the condition for destructive interference.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 3λ is a whole number of wavelengths, which gives constructive interference.

set.explanation_short: White lead, basic lead carbonate 2PbCO₃·Pb(OH)₂, is a heavy white amorphous powder — the property given in the UHS key.

set.explanation_short: N₂ has a triple bond, N≡N, made of one σ bond and two π bonds.
set.explanation_long: Each nitrogen atom has three unpaired 2p electrons. End-on overlap of one pair of p orbitals forms a σ bond, and sideways overlap of the other two perpendicular pairs forms two π bonds, giving the triple bond N≡N. This is why N₂ has a very high bond energy (946 kJ mol⁻¹) and is so unreactive.

explanation_options.a: Correct — the N≡N triple bond is one σ and two π bonds.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — one σ and one π is a double bond, as in O₂.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — only one σ bond can form between the same two atoms.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — two σ bonds cannot exist between the same pair of atoms.

match_question_text: The Kc has following units for the reaction H2(g) + I2(g) ⇋ 2HI (g)

set.explanation_short: For H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), Kc = [HI]²/([H₂][I₂]); the concentration units cancel (mol² dm⁻⁶ over mol² dm⁻⁶), so Kc has no unit.
set.explanation_long: Kc = [HI]²/([H₂][I₂]). The numerator has units (mol dm⁻³)² and the denominator (mol dm⁻³)(mol dm⁻³), so the units cancel completely. In general Kc has units of (mol dm⁻³)^Δn, where Δn is moles of gaseous products minus moles of gaseous reactants; here Δn = 2 − 2 = 0, so Kc is unitless.
set.explanation_trick: Count moles: if both sides of the equation have the same total, Kc has no units.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — mol³ dm⁻⁶ does not arise from this reaction's expression.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — mol dm⁻³ would need one more mole of gas on the product side.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — the units cancel, so no negative powers remain.
explanation_options.d: Correct — Δn = 0, so Kc has no unit.

match_question_text: Choose the CORRECT sentence.
match_option_a: He walked as though he is lame.

set.explanation_short: 'As though' introduces an unreal situation, which takes the subjunctive 'were': 'He walked as though he were lame.'
set.explanation_long: After 'as if' and 'as though', when the clause describes something that is not true (he was not really lame), standard grammar uses the subjunctive 'were' for every person — 'as though he were lame', just as in 'if I were you'. 'Was' is common in informal speech but is not the correct form a grammar test expects. 'Is' breaks the past-tense sequence, and 'may have been' changes the meaning. (The printed UHS key marks B, 'was', but the subjunctive 'were' is the grammatically correct choice.)
set.explanation_trick: Unreal 'as if / as though' → were, whatever the subject.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 'is' breaks the sequence of tenses after the past-tense 'walked'.
explanation_options.b: Informal — 'was' is heard in speech, but the unreal comparison needs the subjunctive 'were'.
explanation_options.c: Correct — 'as though he were lame' uses the subjunctive for an unreal comparison.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 'may have been' changes the meaning to a real possibility.

match_question_text: Type of respiration which involves step by step breakdown of carbon chain molecules in the cell is called:

set.explanation_long: Cellular respiration involves a series of enzymatic reactions (glycolysis, Krebs cycle, electron transport chain) that gradually break down carbon-based fuel molecules like glucose, releasing energy in controlled, stepwise fashion (rather than all at once) and ultimately producing ATP. The printed UHS key marks D (cutaneous respiration), which is gas exchange through the skin, not the breakdown of molecules in cells, so B is kept.

match_question_text: Instrument which is used to measure relative abilities of different pigments to absorb different wavelengths of light is called:

set.explanation_long: A spectrophotometer combines a spectrometer (which isolates specific wavelengths) with a photometer (which measures light intensity), allowing precise measurement of the relative light absorption of pigments (like chlorophyll) at different wavelengths — essential for studying absorption spectra. The printed UHS key marks B (photometer), but a photometer measures only light intensity; comparing absorption across wavelengths needs a spectrophotometer, so D is kept.

match_question_text: Where is the ileocolic sphincter located in your body?
match_option_a: At the junction of esophagus and stomach

set.explanation_short: The ileocolic (ileocaecal) sphincter guards the junction of the ileum and the large intestine.
set.explanation_long: The ileum, the last part of the small intestine, opens into the caecum of the large intestine through the ileocolic sphincter (ileocaecal valve), which lets chyme pass into the colon and prevents backflow. Option D is also broadly true, since the ileum is part of the small intestine, but C names the exact junction and is the answer in the UHS key. The cardiac sphincter guards the oesophagus–stomach junction and the pyloric sphincter the stomach–small intestine junction.
set.explanation_trick: The name tells you the place: ileo-colic = ileum + colon.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — the oesophagus–stomach junction is guarded by the cardiac sphincter.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — the stomach–small intestine junction is guarded by the pyloric sphincter.
explanation_options.c: Correct — the ileocolic sphincter lies where the ileum joins the large intestine.
explanation_options.d: Broadly true but less precise — the sphincter is specifically at the end of the ileum; the key marks C.

match_question_text: The flow of lymph in lymphatic vessels is maintained by:
match_option_a: Heart, activity of smooth muscles and valves

set.explanation_short: Lymph has no pump of its own: it is pushed along by contracting skeletal muscles and breathing movements, while valves stop it flowing backwards.
set.explanation_long: Lymphatic vessels are not connected to the heart's pumping action. Lymph moves because nearby skeletal muscles squeeze the vessels when they contract, and because pressure changes during breathing draw lymph towards the thorax. Numerous one-way valves inside the vessels make sure this squeezing moves lymph only towards the heart.
set.explanation_trick: Lymph flow = muscle squeeze + breathing + valves (no heart).

explanation_options.a: Wrong — the heart does not pump lymph, and skeletal (not smooth) muscle is the main driver.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — the heart does not pump lymph, and valves are left out.
explanation_options.c: Correct — breathing movements, skeletal muscle activity and valves keep lymph flowing.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — the heart does not drive lymph flow, and valves are left out.

match_question_text: Reflexes and instincts type of behaviours respond to which combination /s?
match_option_a: Biological rhythms, territorial, courtship and development

set.explanation_short: Aggression, mating and altruism are standard examples of instinctive (innate) behaviour — the combination chosen in the UHS key.
set.explanation_long: Innate behaviour, which includes reflexes and instincts, is inherited rather than learned, and appears in its complete form the first time it is needed. Textbooks list aggression (defending territory or young), mating behaviour and altruism among such instinctive behaviour patterns. The question wording is unclear, and option D's idea of 'predetermined' responses is related, but it compares behaviour with cell differentiation, which is not behaviour at all; the UHS key marks C.
set.explanation_trick: Instincts are inherited behaviour patterns — think fighting, courting and helping relatives.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — biological rhythms and development are not the combination given for reflexes and instincts.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — this describes a property of responses, not the behaviours in question.
explanation_options.c: Correct (UHS key) — aggression, mating and altruism are instinctive behaviours.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — cell differentiation is a developmental process, not a behaviour.

match_question_text: A typical neuron at rest
match_option_a: Is more positive outside than inside

set.explanation_short: A resting neuron is more positive outside than inside; the inside is about −70 mV relative to the outside.
set.explanation_long: The sodium–potassium pump moves 3 Na⁺ out for every 2 K⁺ in, and the membrane leaks K⁺ out more easily than Na⁺ in. Large negative proteins also stay inside. As a result the outside of the resting membrane is positive and the inside negative, a resting potential of about −70 mV. The polarity reverses briefly during an action potential.
set.explanation_trick: Resting neuron: positive outside, negative inside (−70 mV).

explanation_options.a: Correct — at rest the outside is positive relative to the inside.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — this is reversed; the inside, not the outside, is negative.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — there is a charge difference of about 70 mV across the membrane.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — the charges on the two sides are unequal.

match_question_text: Fungi store surplus food in the form of

set.explanation_short: Fungi store surplus food as glycogen (and oil), like animals — not as starch.
set.explanation_long: Fungi are heterotrophs whose cell walls are made of chitin, and they store excess carbohydrate as glycogen, the same storage polysaccharide animals use, along with lipid droplets. Starch is the storage form of plants and green algae, and cellulose is a structural material, not a food store.
set.explanation_trick: Glycogen storage is one of the ways fungi resemble animals more than plants.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — cellulose is a structural polysaccharide, not a food reserve.
explanation_options.b: Correct — fungi store surplus food as glycogen.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — starch is the food reserve of plants, not fungi.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — fungi do not store starch, so 'Both B and C' is incorrect.
